       TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
       U3 Landowners file this Initial Brief in the above-captioned proceeding and respectfully
show as follows:
                                      I. INTRODUCTION

       U3 Landowners support Route 894, the route recommended by Applicants as the route that
best meets the requirements of the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) and the Public Utility
Commission’s (PUC) substantive rules. U3 Landowners submit this brief in support of Route 894
and in opposition to all routes containing Link U3, including proposed Routes 389, 391, 392, 399,
402, 408, 410, 416, 420, 588, 589, and 592.
       The record demonstrates that Route 894 provides the best overall balance of the objective
routing factors established by PURA and PUC rules. At the hearing, no party advocated for any
U3 route other than a narrow coalition of intervenors who support Route 392, and the record
reflects that this support did not represent any broad consensus among affected landowners,
parties, Applicants, Commission Staff, or the public. Route 894 performs best on major objective
routing metrics—including length, cost, habitable structures, paralleling existing compatible
rights-of-way, riparian areas, and stream crossings. And Route 894 avoids the significant site-

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                   Initial Brief of U3 Landowners
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                    1
 specific impacts that Route 392 would impose on U3 Landowners’ properties. Route 392 should
be rejected because a comprehensive application of the statutory and regulatory routing criteria
favors Route 894. The record demonstrates that:
       1. Neither Applicants nor Staff identified Route 392 or any U3 route as their best-meets
          or recommended route.
       2. Route 894 is $34,299,000 less expensive than Route 392.
       3. Route 392 affects 60% more habitable structures than Route 894.
       4. Route 894 parallels 9.56 more miles of existing compatible rights-of-way than Route
          392.
       5. Route 894 crosses 4.37 fewer miles of riparian areas than Route 392.
       6. Route 894 has 33 fewer stream crossings than Route 392.
       7. Route 894 avoids the extraordinary site-specific harms that Link U3 would impose on
          the U3 Landowners, including: (a) bisection and fragmentation of the ranch across
          multiple tracts; (b) exacerbation of documented access and erosion impacts on steep,
          riparian terrain; (c) permanent sterilization of a valuable sandstone quarry; and (d)
          impacts to the USFWS-designated critical habitat for the Texas pimpleback, a federally
          and state-listed mussel species.
       8. Link U3 was added to the routing analysis after the public participation meetings held
          in June 2025, raising procedural fairness concerns that warrant reduced weight for this
          late-added link—particularly when the Applicant- and Staff-recommended routes
          avoid this link entirely.
       The Route 392 proponents presented novel and untested arguments focused primarily on a
single supposed “advantage” of all Link U3 routes—that they would parallel existing transmission
infrastructure at the Colorado River crossing. Paralleling is just one factor among many that must
be weighed under the multi-factor balancing framework provided by PURA and PUC rules. These
arguments neither overcome Route 894’s superior routing performance nor justify the
extraordinary, avoidable harm Link U3 would impose on U3 Landowners.
       U3 Landowners recognize that the ALJs must review an unusually large record and
substantial briefing from many parties in this proceeding. For that reason, this brief focuses only
on the points that matter most. The Commission’s statutory duty is to select the route that best
meets the overall requirements of PURA and PUC rules. That route is Route 894.

                                     II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

        A.      The Project and Route Selection Process
        Applicants jointly applied to construct a new 765-kV single-circuit transmission line
between Oncor’s existing Bell County East Switch and LCRA TSC’s existing Big Hill 345-kV
Substation. The proposed transmission line would traverse Central and West Texas, with a study
area of approximately 6,267 square miles.
        Applicants conducted a comprehensive Environmental Assessment (EA) and Alternative
Route Analysis to evaluate the potential transmission line routes. The EA applied 36 specific
environmental and land use criteria in order to operationalize the route selection criteria from
PURA and PUC rules. Based on this comprehensive analysis, Applicants identified Route 894 as
the route that best meets the statutory and regulatory requirements.
        B.      U3 Landowners Property and Ownership
        U3 Landowners own and/or reside on property located on, adjacent to, or in close proximity
to proposed Link U3. As reflected in Chris Rowntree’s direct testimony and the statements of
position filed by other U3 Landowners, these properties are similarly situated Hill Country
properties characterized by rolling and rugged terrain, wooded areas, restored native grasslands,
creek and draw systems, limestone features, riparian habitat, and elevated scenic views. Their
combination of steep slopes, stream crossings, perennial watercourses, and sensitive land uses
makes them especially vulnerable to additional fragmentation by linear infrastructure.1
        3 Trees Ranch comprises approximately 955 acres of property in Lampasas County. The
Rowntree family has deep historical ties to the Lampasas area dating back to the 1840s, when
family members were among the earliest settlers in the region. The reacquisition of land in the
same area was pursued to preserve the family connection to the land, protect the property from
development, restore a family legacy, and create a lasting place to pass down the Texas ranching
way of life for generations.2 This family ranch is characterized by substantial topographic relief,
steep terrain, and extensive riparian corridors associated with the Colorado River and its
tributaries. The property includes areas identified in the Application as Tracts 4925, 4926, 4927,

        C.      Link U3 and Effect of U3 Routes on U3 Landowners’ Properties
        Link U3 is a proposed transmission line segment that would bisect 3 Trees Ranch and other
U3 Landowner properties. Link U3 is not part of Route 894, the Applicants’ best-meets route.
Link U3 is not part of Route 487, PUC Staff’s recommended route. Link U3 is included in 12
alternative routes proposed by the Applicants: Routes 389, 391, 392, 399, 402, 408, 410, 416, 420,
588, 589, and 592.
        Construction of Link U3 would require the clearing of many ancient live oaks, burr oaks,
pecans, and other hardwoods. The proposed line would traverse the central portions of multiple
U3 Landowners’ properties. Much of the proposed route for U3 runs through steep topography
and erosion-sensitive riparian areas.6 A significant portion of the western Lampasas County
watershed drains through these waterways before reaching the Colorado River.7
        D.      Existing Right-of-Way Abuse History
        A small existing transmission line crosses 3 Trees Ranch for approximately 7,400 feet.
The line is so old that its date of installation is unknown, but it is believed the line was originally
69kV and later upfitted to 138kV. The access and maintenance easement for this transmission line
is approximately 75 feet wide, and crosses Antelope Creek, Cottonwood Branch, Lope-A-Long
Draw, and numerous unnamed stream beds and ravines.8 The record reflects that since the
Rowntrees’ acquisition of the land in 1989, the family has repeatedly observed LCRA TSC and its
contractors trespassing outside the legally granted easement for inspection, maintenance, and tree
clearing. This repeated trespassing has caused damage to 3 Trees Ranch, resulting in a chain of

        The terrain demonstrates why Link U3 is uniquely problematic. At Antelope Creek and

3 Trees Ranch. 12 A new 200-foot 765-kV right-of-way would more than double the corridor width

        E.       Quarry Sterilization Impacts
        As testified by Mr. Rowntree, Tract 4928 includes an open sandstone quarry located
directly below the proposed Link U3 easement.13 A new utility easement bisecting that quarry
footprint would permanently remove recoverable sandstone reserves from productive use. Even
if the impact were limited to that strip, the easement would sterilize the recoverable sandstone
reserves within that area. Blasting, excavation, and safety setbacks associated with transmission
infrastructure could expand the affected area, potentially increasing the sterilized acreage to
approximately 10 to 15 acres.14
        Based on Hill Country sandstone sale prices, operator costs, and net-margin scenarios, the
undiscounted gross sale value of saleable material potentially sterilized within the representative
strip is approximately $11.8 million to $27.7 million, assuming a 30-foot recoverable thickness.15
Even under conservative assumptions, sterilization of quarry reserves would be a material
economic impact far beyond the ordinary grazing or surface-use impacts normally associated with
a linear easement. The EA does not address this quarry sterilization impact.

         F.       Critical Habitat Crossing and Ecologically Significant Stream Segments
        Link U3 crosses USFWS critical habitat for the Texas pimpleback, a federally and state-
listed mussel species.16 The Environmental Assessment identifies the Texas pimpleback as a
species associated with perennial streams, tributaries, and major waterways in the Colorado River
basin. These mussels inhabit sand, gravel, silt, mud, and cobble substrates in flowing water and
depend on stable flow regimes and clean substrates.17                 Furthermore, in a study area of
approximately 6,267 square miles—roughly four times the size of Rhode Island—the EA indicates
there are only eight Ecologically Significant Stream Segments, and U3 contains one of them.18
        G.       Notice and Public Input: Late Addition of Link U3
        Applicants’ witness Marusak confirmed that U3 was not on the preliminary route maps
presented at the public meetings, that the 520-foot public-meeting mailing list therefore could not
have been based on U3, and that Applicants did not hold a supplemental public-participation
meeting where landowners newly affected by U3 were shown the route map and asked for input.19
Applicant witness Wells agreed that a landowner whose property was not on the preliminary route
map and who resided outside the study area would have received neither mailed notice of the
public-participation meetings nor newspaper notice where the landowner resides.20 Mr. Rowntree
and other U3 Landowners reside outside the study area, and the received neither mailed notice nor
newspaper notice of the public participation meetings.


                                              III. ARGUMENT

        A.       The Commission Must Apply Multi-Factor Balancing in Route Selection

                 1.  The Statutory and Regulatory Framework Requires Multi-Factor
                     Balancing
        PURA and the Commission’s rules establish a comprehensive routing framework requiring
the Commission to balance multiple factors, including land use, environmental integrity,
aesthetics, cultural resources, and cost. This statutory structure reflects a deliberate legislative

 choice to prevent any single factor from dominating the route selection process. At the hearing,
the applicant panel, Smitherman, Anderson, and Scott agree that no factor should be weighted over
the others.21 Rather, the Commission must weigh the totality of the circumstances to identify the
route that best serves the overall public interest and meets the statutory requirements. The
framework is inherently wholistic and multi-dimensional, requiring an assessment of how each
proposed route performs across numerous diverse factors.

                2. Commission Precedent Requires Route-Wide Analysis, Not Single-
                   Factor Preference
        Recent Commission orders in transmission-line routing cases confirm that the route
recommendation in this case should be driven by the objective, route-wide record under PURA
§ 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). The Commission’s recent decisions show that a
proposed route should not be selected because a single group of landowners prefers it, because it
avoids a localized concern, or because it performs better on one selected routing characteristic.
The route must best balance the statutory and regulatory criteria as a whole.
        That principle is particularly important here because Route 392 is being advanced largely
as a party-preference route. Neither the Applicants nor Commission Staff identified Route 392—
or any route using Link U3—as the route that best meets the Commission’s routing criteria. The
Applicants selected Route 894. Staff selected Route 487. Route 392 is not a compromise between
those recommendations; it is a materially worse alternative on the core objective metrics.
Compared with Route 894, Route 392 is more expensive, longer, and affects 51 additional
habitable structures. And the broader U3 route family does not solve that problem: every filed U3
route is more expensive than Route 894, the least expensive U3 route affects 141 habitable
structures, and the U3 route with the fewest habitable structures still affects more habitable
structures than Route 894 while costing substantially more.
        Docket 58276
        The Commission’s order in Docket No. 58276 is directly instructive, as it provides the
modern four-prong test for evaluating whether a one route is superior to an alternative. In that
docket, SOAH recommended Route 28. The Commission rejected SOAH’s recommendation,
finding the PFD did not properly apply the PURA and PUC routing factors and assigned too much

habitable structures, cost less, was shorter, and was superior in a majority of the objective

       The lesson for this case is direct: a PFD that elevates a localized preference over stronger
route-wide objective metrics risks the same correction at the Commission level. Route 392
presents that same problem, but more starkly. Route 894 satisfies each of the four Docket 58276
override prongs versus Route 392 by wider margins than Route 26 did versus Route 28. Route
392 asks the Commission to spend more money to build a longer route that affects 51 more
habitable structures, based largely on an untested Colorado River-crossing theory. Docket 58276
confirms the PFD should avoid that error and recommend Route 894 as the route that best balances
the objective routing criteria across the route as a whole. This is not stale precedent from a
differently composed Commission. The Docket 58276 order was signed three months ago by
Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners Jackson, Hjaltman, and Johnson—four Commissioners
who remain on the Commission today.
       Docket No. 55728
       Docket No. 55728 is a cautionary example for this case: the Commission recently rejected
a SOAH recommendation that elevated localized concerns about proposed development over
stronger route-wide objective metrics, including fewer habitable structures. That lesson matters
here because Route 392 invites the ALJs to make the same kind of error—elevating speculative
future development on Route 392 over 51 additional existing habitable structures, increased cost,
length, and poorer performance in total compatible ROW. In 55728, SOAH recommended
Route S. The Commission nevertheless rejected the ALJs’ recommended route and approved an
alternate route because it best balanced the routing factors. After two remands to give the parties
an opportunity to provide sufficient evidentiary support for Route S, Chairman Gleeson concluded
they still had not met this burden.
       The Chairman’s Memorandum in Docket 55728 explains his reasoning in verbatim
language directly applicable to the present proceeding. Gleeson wrote: “My primary concerns
with route S are its impact on habitable structures and the apparent intent of the parties in agreeing
on Route S—to reduce the impact of the transmission line on the future development of property

 owned by Vise Oaks.”22 The Chairman continued: “Commission precedent is clear that when
making routing decisions, the Commission may not prioritize a landowner’s concerns about future
development of his undeveloped property over existing constraints.”23 Gleeson cited three earlier
Commission decisions establishing this principle: Docket No. 39479,24 Docket No. 45866,25 and
Docket No. 48358.26 Notably—and dispositively for the present case—the Chairman expressly
acknowledged that the route recommended by the ALJs but ultimately rejected by the Commission
had lower cost and paralleled existing corridors for more of its length, yet the Commission
nonetheless approved an alternate route because the four-factor balance favored that route.27
        That same problem confronts the ALJ presiding over the instant proceeding. Solana’s
advocacy for Route 392 is really its opposition to Route 894, which is grounded in future
development plans, not existing habitable structures. At the hearing, Solana witness Alexander
admitted on cross-examination that by the end of 2025 and as of the June 11, 2026 hearing, the
developer had not built a single home at the Solana Development.28 Route 392 would elevate
those future development plans by selecting a more expensive, longer route, and shifting the line
onto a route with 51 additional habitable structures—including U3 Landowners—with existing
residences, ranch uses, riparian features, access constraints, critical-habitat concerns, and site-
specific impacts. Docket No. 55728 confirms that the PFD in this case should reject that approach
and recommend Route 894.

proponents’ argument in this proceeding.            The Route 392 proponents base their case on

combined with lower cost—was insufficient to override the four-factor balance when the other
route was superior on habitable structures and other factors. The same analysis applies here with
even greater force: Route 894 is over 34 million dollars less expensive than Route 392, affects 51
fewer habitable structures, is 5.8 miles shorter, doesn’t cross the Colorado River at an ESSS, and

              3.     Transmission-Line Paralleling Is Not Dispositive
        The Route 392 proponents argue that Route 392 should be selected because it parallels an
existing transmission corridor at the Colorado River crossing. That argument misstates the role of
paralleling in the routing analysis. Paralleling existing infrastructure may be relevant, but it is not
a mandate that overrides the full statutory and regulatory framework.
        PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require the Commission to consider
multiple paralleling and routing factors, including whether a route parallels or uses existing
electric-facility rights-of-way, other compatible rights-of-way such as roads, highways, railroads,
or telephone utility rights-of-way, property lines or other natural or cultural features, and whether
the route conforms with prudent avoidance. The statute and rule do not use the Route 392
proponents’ preferred phrase “existing compatible infrastructure,” and they do not elevate
transmission-line paralleling above property-boundary paralleling, cost, habitable structures,
environmental integrity, cultural resources, aesthetics, or other routing considerations.
        The Route 392 proponents’ effort to narrow the analysis to physical infrastructure is
therefore not a neutral application of the routing criteria. It is a results-driven attempt to isolate
the one metric on which Route 392 performs relatively well while excluding a statutory factor—
property-boundary paralleling—on which Route 894 performs substantially better. Applicants

           Route 392 looks better only if the analysis is narrowed to selected infrastructure categories
and property-boundary paralleling is removed from consideration. But the Commission is not
limited to infrastructure paralleling, and Route 392’s proponents cannot improve their preferred
route by discarding a statutory routing factor simply because it favors Route 894. The Commission
must evaluate paralleling as part of the route-wide balancing required by PURA and the
Commission’s rules, not as a dispositive preference for one localized river crossing.

                   4.  Route 894 Performs Better than any U3 Route and Certainly Route 392
                       Under the Routing Factors
           The record establishes that Route 894 provides the best overall balance of the
Commission’s routing criteria, particularly when compared to routes containing Link U3. The
comparison between Route 894 and Route 392 is not close. Route 894 outperforms Route 392 on
the major routing criteria the Commission has repeatedly treated as most important: cost, prudent
avoidance, route length, and use of existing compatible rights-of-way. Every Link U3 route would
cost materially more than Route 894; Route 392 would impact 60% more habitable structures; and
